---
title: "Linkage disequilibrium and what it decides for you"
subtitle: "Why the resolution of a fine-mapping analysis is set by the population, not by the method"
---

Every association a GWAS reports is an association with a *region*, not with a
variant. The scan tests markers, and a marker is informative only because it is
correlated with whatever is actually causal nearby. That correlation is linkage
disequilibrium, and it is the reason the method works at all.

It is also the reason the method stops working at a certain point. LD is what
lets a genotyping array of 400,000 markers stand in for three billion bases; it
is equally what prevents the resulting signal from being narrowed to one variant.
The same property does both, and no analysis can have the first without the
second.

This page is about the second half of that trade, because it is the half that
tutorials skip. It concerns how the guide's fine-mapping result should be read,
and it makes a case for ancestral diversity in genetic studies that rests on
resolution rather than on fairness.

---

## 01 - LD is a property of a population, not of the genome

**Why.** There is no such thing as *the* linkage disequilibrium between two
variants. There is the LD between them in a particular population, and it can
differ severalfold between populations at the same pair of sites.

The reason is demographic history. LD is created by drift and destroyed by
recombination, so the balance between them depends on effective population size.
A population that has been small has more LD, because its members are closer
relatives and fewer recombination events separate them; a population that has
been large has less, because recombination has had more independent
opportunities to break associations apart
[doi:10.1534/genetics.114.166454]{.mark}. Bottlenecks and expansions leave
distinct and long-lasting signatures on the whole LD curve, and those signatures
persist for hundreds of generations after the demographic event that caused them
[doi:10.1534/genetics.114.166454]{.mark}.

For human populations, one consequence dominates everything else. African
populations have the largest ancestral effective size and did not pass through
the out-of-Africa bottleneck; non-African populations did. LD therefore extends
further in Europe and East Asia than in Africa, and this has been documented at
genome scale since the first surveys
[PMID:11346797]{.mark} [PMID:11967554]{.mark}.

---

## 02 - Measuring it on the demonstration data

**Why.** The statement above is standard and you should not take it on trust
when you can check it in the dataset you are already using.

```bash
bash scripts/07_linkage_disequilibrium/01_ld_decay.sh
```

The script computes pairwise r² among common variants across the *ABO* region,
separately within each ancestry group, and averages by physical distance.

| Distance between variants | European | African | East Asian |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 0-10 kb | 0.272 | **0.184** | 0.344 |
| 10-25 kb | 0.122 | **0.063** | 0.173 |
| 25-50 kb | 0.047 | **0.022** | 0.089 |
| 50-100 kb | 0.031 | **0.010** | 0.029 |
| 100-200 kb | 0.018 | 0.006 | 0.013 |

Read the African column against the other two. At 25 to 50 kb, average r² in the
African group is less than half the European value and about a quarter of the
East Asian one. The ordering is the same at every distance, and it is the
ordering that population history predicts.

::: {.callout-note title="What this is not"}
This is 288 African individuals at one locus on one array, not a genome-wide
estimate of LD decay. The magnitudes here should not be quoted as such. What the
comparison establishes is the *direction and the size of the difference between
groups measured in the same way on the same variants*, which is the only thing
the next section needs.
:::

---

## 03 - The consequence: resolution is set before you choose a method

**Why.** Fine mapping asks which variant in a region is causal. It can only
distinguish variants that the data distinguish. Two variants in perfect LD carry
identical information about every phenotype, so no amount of statistical
sophistication, and no increase in sample size, will ever separate them.

The demonstration dataset makes this concrete. Counting variants in strong LD
(r² > 0.8) with the causal variant, within each group:

| | European | African | East Asian |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Variants indistinguishable from the causal one | 11 | **1** | 11 |

This single table explains the fine-mapping result of
[Fine mapping](../06_finemapping_annotation/06_finemapping_annotation.qmd)
before any Bayes factor is computed. The European credible set contains eleven
variants because Europe contains eleven variants that behave identically at this
locus. The credible set is not eleven wide because the method is weak; it is
eleven wide because the population is.

In the African group the same locus resolves to a single variant. The causal
variant is separable there and is not separable in Europe, and that difference
was fixed tens of thousands of years before anyone collected a sample.

::: {.callout-important title="A small credible set is not a resolved locus"}
The two statements sound alike and are not. A credible set of eleven variants
spanning 12 kb looks tidy, and a reader may take the tidiness as success. It is
not: it is a compact haplotype block, and the set is small because the region is
small, not because the analysis resolved anything within it. In the African
group the same locus resolves to one variant, and that is resolution. Report the span, the number of variants, and the local LD alongside the
posterior probabilities, so that a reader can tell a resolved locus from a
region where resolution was never available
[doi:10.1038/nrg1123]{.mark}.
:::

---

## 04 - Three practical consequences

**The LD reference must match the ancestry of the analysis.** Summary-statistic
fine-mapping and conditional analysis both need an LD matrix, and if that matrix
comes from a population with different LD than the study sample, the method is
being told correlations that do not hold in the data. This produces credible
sets that are confidently wrong rather than honestly wide. Where the study is
multi-ancestry, one reference cannot serve, and per-stratum LD is required.

**Diversity buys resolution, not only equity.** The argument for including
non-European participants in genetic studies is usually made on grounds of
fairness, and that argument is sufficient on its own. But it is not the only one.
The table above shows a locus that is unresolvable in Europe and resolvable in
Africa, in the same data, with the same method. Shorter LD is more information
per variant. A study that recruits only Europeans is not merely leaving other
populations unserved; it is discarding the resolution that would have answered
its own question [PMID:11037333]{.mark}.

**Trans-ancestry analysis helps when the strata are large enough to be heard.**
In this demonstration, combining the three groups moves the causal variant to
first place in the credible set but barely shrinks the set, because the African
group that could separate the variants contributes 288 people against 608
Europeans. The mechanism is real and the sample is too small to exploit it. That
is the honest reading, and it is also the argument for building consortia in
which non-European strata are large enough to change the answer rather than
large enough to be mentioned.

---

## Key decisions on this page

- Whether the LD reference panel matches the ancestry of each analysed stratum,
  and what was done where it could not.
- Whether reported credible sets are accompanied by their span and by the local
  LD, so that width can be attributed to the population rather than to the
  method.
- Whether the study design treats ancestral diversity as a source of resolution
  at the analysis stage, or only as a recruitment target.

Next: [Fine mapping](../06_finemapping_annotation/06_finemapping_annotation.qmd),
where these constraints determine the result.
